title: Resource-bounded controllability benchmarking of open quantum systems
authors: Yule Mayevsky, Akram Youssry, Alberto Peruzzo
abstract: This paper develops a resource-bounded framework for evaluating practical controllability in open quantum systems using a trained graybox response model. Rather than treating controllability as a binary property of an idealised Hamiltonian model, the proposed approach evaluates the best-achievable process fidelity over a finite, hardware-realisable pulse family under explicit control constraints. The graybox model retains the known coherent dynamics while learning control-dependent open-system distortions from pulse-response data. The resulting surrogate predictions are used to reconstruct the implemented processes and compare them with Haar-random target gates. Practical controllability is then characterised through the distribution of best-achievable infidelities and an area-based summary metric. The framework is demonstrated for a driven qubit under closed-system, classical-noise, and combined quantum-plus-classical-noise dynamics, with pulse amplitude and inverse Gaussian width used as the control-resource coordinates. The results show how finite control resources and open-system noise jointly constrain the gate performance attainable by the chosen pulse family.
summary: The authors introduce a novel, resource-bounded framework to benchmark the true controllability of open quantum systems. They use a graybox machine learning model trained on experimental data to predict gate fidelity under realistic constraints like limited pulse amplitude and bandwidth. This allows researchers to map out an 'operational map' showing exactly how much performance is lost due to noise versus hardware limitations.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of evaluating practical quantum gate fidelity in open systems, moving beyond idealized Hamiltonian models to account for hardware limitations.
main_result: Controllability is characterized by resource-bounded surfaces (e.g., amplitude vs. bandwidth) that quantify achievable process fidelity under explicit noise and control constraints.
method: A graybox machine learning model is trained on probing data to predict open-system distortions, allowing the reconstruction of implemented quantum channels for fidelity benchmarking.
model_or_system: The system is an open quantum system (demonstrated on a driven qubit) whose dynamics are governed by Hamiltonians incorporating drift, control fields, and various noise sources (classical or combined quantum/classical).
key_observables: Process fidelity; distribution of best-achievable infidelities; Controllability Metric (CM); two-dimensional controllability surfaces.
important_parameters: Control resources such as pulse amplitude ($A_{cap}$) and bandwidth ($	ext{BW}_{cap}$); noise parameters ($\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \gamma$ rates).
main_assumptions: The graybox model is assumed valid only over the bounded region of control space defined by its training data; results are conditional on the chosen pulse family parametrization.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate workflow (data collection to fidelity evaluation) and, crucially, two-dimensional controllability surfaces showing how noise deforms the achievable gate performance landscape as a function of resource caps.
paper_structure: The paper develops a framework by first defining the problem (practical vs. ideal control), then detailing the graybox ML methodology for channel reconstruction under constraints, and finally presenting quantitative benchmarks across various noise regimes using area-based metrics.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly practical, data-driven metric for assessing quantum hardware performance that explicitly incorporates resource costs (like pulse power or bandwidth) alongside environmental decoherence.

For each variant, the trained graybox predicts the corresponding dynamics, including both the coherent unitary part and the noise contribution, allowing the effective implemented channel to be reconstructed. Distributions and empirical cumulative distribution functions of the best achievable infidelity 1 −Fmax(G) over the Haar-random target-gate ensemble. The amplitude study varies the waveform amplitude resource, while the Gaussian-width study varies the common temporal width σ, which acts as the bandwidth-related resource coordinate. The shaded regions in the CDF panels represent the area used to calculate the corresponding controllability measure.
